children: Central bankers risk committing "multiple policy errors" if they treat inflation expectations as a standalone policy objective, UBS Chief Economist Paul Donovan warned in a research note published Wednesday.

With the ongoing Gulf war pushing headline inflation higher and Google search interest in "inflation" running nearly double the levels seen during the post-pandemic price spike, policymakers are once again fixating on survey-based expectations—but Donovan argued this approach ignores how fundamentally social media has reshaped public perceptions.

Consumer views on future prices have become dramatically unmoored from reality: in nearly 50 years of the University of Michigan sentiment survey, Americans have expected inflation below 2% for exactly eight months, while actual inflation came in below that threshold for 138 months. The distortion has reached new extremes, with almost 30% of recent U.S. respondents claiming to expect inflation above 15%—a level the country has never experienced since tracking began in 1978.

Yet, expectations without the power to act are "largely irrelevant," Donovan contended. For consumer inflation expectations to matter economically, workers need sufficient pay bargaining power to trigger a wage-price spiral—something evident in the unusual labor markets of 2022 but conspicuously absent now. UBS analysis shows wage growth is not keeping pace with anticipated price increases, indicating workers lack the leverage to translate fears into higher paychecks. Nor are consumers accelerating purchases or drawing down savings ahead of expected price rises.

Corporate expectations face similar constraints: while companies may anticipate cost increases and attempt to pass them on, this requires pricing power that not all firms possess. German manufacturers, for instance, responded to expected energy cost increases after Russia's invasion of Ukraine by becoming more efficient—a disinflationary response.

The one group whose expectations truly matter is financial investors, who face "fewer barriers to translating expectations into actions that have consequences," Donovan wrote. When bond investors expect 3% inflation, they demand compensation built into yields—regardless of current inflation—creating immediate burdens for borrowers whose revenues grow only at actual inflation rates.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh—drawing from his background on Wall Street—has long been a vocal advocate for incorporating forward-looking asset prices and market-based measures into monetary policymaking. He has emphasized that such market measures offer real-time, "skin in the game" signals that often complement or outperform backward-looking economic models and abstract consumer surveys.

Donovan's prescription: "For now, central bankers should probably disregard the inflation expectations of consumer and corporate surveys, and focus specifically on financial market expectations when thinking about policy setting."

title: Why inflation expectations matter less than central bankers think
